identity.title: How Reliable is Language Model Micro-Benchmarking?

problem.claim: The paper asks whether micro-benchmarks can rank models as consistently as full benchmarks, and whether they outperform random subsets.

gap.claim: The authors report that micro-benchmarks are unreliable in many scenarios, challenging prior suggestions that as few as 10 examples may suffice.

contributions.claim: Introduces a measure relating micro-benchmark ranking reliability to model performance differences on the full benchmark.
Uses the measure to identify which model pairs can be ranked correctly and analyze the trade-off between benchmark size and reliability.
Provides actionable guidance for navigating evaluation efficiency versus reliability.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors state that they introduce a meta-evaluation measure for micro-benchmarking.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that no micro-benchmarking method can consistently rank model pairs separated by 3.5 accuracy points on MMLU-Pro or 4 points on BIG-bench Hard.
They report that consistently ranking relatively similar models often requires up to 250 examples, after which random sampling is competitive with existing methods.
For 8B instruction-tuned models on MMLU-Pro with 25-example micro-benchmarks, more than half of pairwise comparisons are reported as unlikely to be preserved.

narrative_sequence.summary: Micro-benchmarking is presented as a way to reduce the time and cost of language-model development by evaluating a small subset of existing benchmarks.
The paper examines consistency against full benchmarks and performance relative to random data-point selection.
It introduces a meta-evaluation measure that links ranking ability to full-benchmark performance differences and supports pair-specific analysis.
The authors report poor reliability at small sizes, with substantially larger samples often needed and random sampling becoming competitive.
The work offers guidance for balancing evaluation efficiency and reliability.

source_observation.claim: The abstract evaluates ranking reliability as a function of model performance difference and benchmark size, rather than treating reliability as a single overall property.

lessons.interpretation: This framing makes evaluation claims more operational and exposes where a method fails.
lessons.application: Report reliability thresholds separately by model-gap size and sample budget when presenting a reduced evaluation method.
lessons.exception: This may be unsuitable when the intended use is calibration, generation quality, or another objective not reducible to pairwise ranking.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the datasets, sampling procedures, number of model pairs, or statistical criterion underlying “consistently” and “likely.”
It does not identify which micro-benchmarking methods were compared or provide aggregate performance figures.
